name: Tok Pisin
variant: Standard Tok Pisin of Papua New Guinea (careful town speech, with the predicate marker i written; spelling as in Mihalic's Jacaranda dictionary and the Tok Pisin Bible)
script: Latin (no extra letters); left to right
basis: Dutton and Thomas, A New Course in Tok Pisin (Pacific Linguistics D-67, 1985), grammar order of units 1–5, which ANU's TOKP1002 Tok Pisin 1 recommends
src: Tom Dutton with Dicks Thomas, A New Course in Tok Pisin (New Guinea Pidgin), Pacific Linguistics D-67, ANU 1985, open-access PDF via core.ac.uk: read the contents (grammar points of units 1–13) and the text of units 1–2 (pronouns, predicate marker i, pronunciation, spelling, dialogue situations); later units only through the contents list. Not opened: the Peace Corps Tok Pisin course (ERIC ED401761) and the ANU repository copy of Dutton and Thomas; both downloads were refused. Only a catalogue description of the Peace Corps workbook (Bajao 1991) was read
note: The grammar order follows Dutton and Thomas units 1–5 (pronouns, i, stap, bilong; possession, laik, verbless sentences, numbers; dual/trial, questions, pinis, plural nouns, -im; bai, save, time and days; i stap, inap, bin). Placing the lessons on long, -pela, negation, commands, family (brata / susa) and directions, splitting numbers from shopping, and moving dual and trial pronouns later are my own judgment and common course practice; the survival topics match the situations of the book's dialogues (greeting in Boroko, the market, a club, asking the way, travel by bus and plane). Device voices for tpi are not checked and probably do not exist.
hardest: Words that look like English but mean something else: save (know how to, usually), stap (be somewhere), bagarap (broken), pinis (done)
Two words for 'we': yumi (you and me) and mipela (us, not you), plus dual and trial forms such as mitupela
The little markers English lacks: i before the verb after em, ol, mipela; -im on verbs with an object; -pela on adjectives and numbers
brata and susa are counted from the speaker's sex: a man's brata is his brother, a woman's brata is her sister

items: Sounds and spelling: five vowels, ai and au, unaspirated p, t, k, and f / p, v / b
Greetings: Moning, Apinun, Gutnait, Lukim yu
Pronouns: mi, yu, em, yumi, mipela, yupela, ol
The predicate marker i: Em i tisa, Ol i wokabaut (but Mi wokabaut)
Introducing yourself: Nem bilong mi…, Mi bilong Amerika
stap: be somewhere, live (Mi stap long Lae)
long: the all-purpose preposition (long haus, long Mosbi)
bilong: possession (haus bilong mi) and purpose
Questions: wanem, husat, we, hamas, olsem wanem
Negation with no: Mi no save, Mi no gat mani
Numbers and money: wan, tu, tri, ten; kina and toea
-pela on adjectives and counted things: gutpela, bikpela, tupela
laik: want to (Mi laik baim kaukau)
At the market and ordering: Em i kostim hamas?, Bia plis
Verbs with an object and -im: lukim, baim, and kaikai with no -im
Future with bai: Bai mi go long maket
save: know how to, and things done usually (Mi save wok long Mande)
Telling the time and days: Em i wanem taim nau?, Mande, Fraide, Sande
Going on now: verb + i stap (Em i slip i stap)
Past with bin: Mi bin go long Lae
inap: can, be able (Inap yu salim wanpela taksi i kam?)
More than one: ol haus, and two or three people (mitupela, yutupela, mitripela)
Family: papa, mama, pikinini, and brata / susa counted from the speaker
Directions and travel: stret, han kais, han sut; long bas, long balus
Commands and requests: Kam!, Yu no ken…, plis
